strategies.intent: Fuse avgpool into the transposed-convolution producer to bypass the pooled intermediate and improve locality on the real bottleneck.
strategies.summary: The phase-2 champion only improved the fused post-op path, while NCU still shows the dominant `convolveNd_dgrad` kernel with very low SM throughput (~11.5%), low active warps (~32.7%), high L2 utilization (~85.4%), long-scoreboard stalls (~0.32), and a strong register limit (122 regs/thread). That points to the conv-transpose path, not the post-op chain, as the next lever. For the fixed execution facts (`pool_kernel_size=2`, `kernel_size=3`, `stride=2`, `padding=1`, `output_padding=1`), a custom kernel that reads the source once, performs the 2x2x2 average on the fly, and accumulates directly into the transposed-conv output can cut one full tensor materialization and shift more reuse into shared memory/L1.
implementation_hints: Keep ModelNew I/O unchanged and replace only the `avg_pool3d -> conv_transpose3d` internal path when dtype/layout/shape match the fixed benchmark regime.
Exploit the known pooling factor of 2 to compute each pooled input value from an 8-element local window before feeding the transposed-conv accumulation.
Tile over output NCDHW so each block reuses pooled source voxels and relevant filter slices from shared memory or read-only cache.
Retain the existing PyTorch/cuDNN fallback for unsupported shapes, non-float32, or non-contiguous tensors.
Preserve stride/padding/output_padding semantics exactly and guard all spatial boundaries.
strategies.expected_gain: High if the benchmark shape is stable; likely larger than further post-op tweaks because it attacks the kernel still dominating runtime.
risk_notes: Highest implementation complexity among the options.
A custom transposed-conv path can lose to cuDNN on some shapes if tiling is not tuned well.
Numerical parity must be checked carefully because the pooling is moved across the implementation boundary, even though semantics stay the same.
memory_methods: Stage source tiles and filter tiles in shared memory.
mutation_axes: specialization to the fixed pool/stride/kernel tuple
forbidden_patterns: Do not change module parameters or output layout.
Do not reorder pooling and transposed convolution semantically.
Do not drop boundary guards for pooled or deconvolution indices.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Targets the stated bottleneck and removes an intermediate tensor, so upside is real for this fixed-shape benchmark. Risk is high because fused pool+deconv indexing and boundary semantics are easy to get wrong, but value is still strong if shape-guarded.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Directly attacks the dominant convolveNd_dgrad bottleneck by fusing avgpool into the conv-transpose producer, eliminating one tensor materialization and improving spatial reuse. Expected gain is the highest of any strategy here. Score docked from 5 because custom transposed-conv tiling is the hardest kernel in this suite to get right â numerical parity, boundary guards, and matching cuDNN's already-tuned throughput on other shapes all raise implementation risk substantially.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Fusing avgpool into a custom conv_transpose3d kernel is theoretically optimal but carries extremely high implementation risk and complexity. It is unlikely to beat cuDNN without significant tuning.

strategies.intent: Search for a better backend path for `ConvTranspose3d` via explicit layout/algorithm dispatch rather than spending more effort on the already-plateaued post-op kernel.
strategies.summary: The selected and root NCU profiles are effectively unchanged for the main conv-transpose kernel, and the current champion's gains came only from reducing launches after it. The dominant kernel is register-limited and latency-bound, so a different cuDNN engine may outperform the current one. Introduce a shape-guarded dispatch that tries a channels-last-3d / NDHWC path or an alternate cuDNN algorithm, then caches the fastest choice for the benchmark shape.
implementation_hints: Add a small shape-keyed dispatch/cache helper so the first run can pick among a narrow set of safe conv-transpose variants and later runs reuse the winner.
Evaluate an explicit channels-last-3d path only when both input and weights can be converted cheaply and the spatial volume is large enough to amortize the layout change.
Keep the current fused post-op extension unchanged; only swap the producer feeding it.
Prefer backend selection using official ATen/cuDNN entrypoints rather than a full custom kernel when possible.
Gate the optimization to the benchmark's fixed parameter tuple and contiguous tensors to avoid broad regressions.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate; if the current cuDNN engine is a poor fit, a different algorithm/layout could improve occupancy or reduce scoreboard stalls without rewriting the convolution math.
risk_notes: Layout conversion can erase gains if done every iteration on small tensors.
Channels-last-3d support and performance vary by GPU/cuDNN version.
Autotune or algorithm-picking logic adds startup overhead and must be cached.
memory_methods: Use layout conversion only behind profitability guards.
forbidden_patterns: Do not permanently change public tensor layout expectations.
Do not enable broad autotune without caching.
Do not assume channels-last is always faster for transposed convolution.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Good risk-adjusted option: tries safer backend/layout dispatch before committing to a custom deconv kernel. Caching and narrow shape guards keep regressions contained, though layout-conversion overhead could erase gains on some systems.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Algorithm/layout dispatch for the conv-transpose via cuDNN is a low-implementation-risk lever that could help if the current engine is a poor fit for the shape. Gain is speculative and architecture-dependent; the dispatch-and-cache overhead must not dominate single-iteration benchmarks. A pragmatic intermediate step with a meaningful but bounded ceiling.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Exploring layout dispatch (e.g., channels_last_3d) for cuDNN is a low-code, high-reward approach, though the overhead of layout conversion must be carefully managed.

strategies.intent: Reduce global memory reads from 3 to 2 by fusing the max and sum reductions using the online softmax algorithm.
strategies.summary: Implement a 2-pass online softmax in the custom CUDA kernel to reduce memory bandwidth bottleneck.
implementation_hints: Combine the first two passes of the kernel into a single pass.
Maintain `local_max` and `local_sum` per thread. For each clamped value `v`, update using `new_max = fmaxf(local_max, v)` and `local_sum = local_sum * expf(local_max - new_max) + expf(v - new_max)`.
Use warp shuffles (`__shfl_down_sync`) with the same merge logic to perform the block-wide reduction efficiently.
Precompute the scaling factor `float factor = (1.0f / global_sum) * scale[c];` before the final write pass to save redundant multiplications.
strategies.expected_gain: Significant reduction in global memory traffic (33% fewer reads for the custom kernel), leading to lower latency.
risk_notes: Care must be taken to avoid precision issues during the online sum update.
Warp shuffle logic requires exact synchronization and correct mask usage.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Solid optimization for the fused softmax tail and technically sound, but the profile says the transposed-convolution producer still dominates runtime. Useful as an incremental follow-up, not the highest-value next move.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Proposes a 2-pass online softmax to cut global memory reads. The problem is the post-op chain is not the bottleneck â NCU confirms the dominant runtime is convolveNd_dgrad. The online softmax is a well-known technique, but applying it to a secondary kernel that is not limiting overall latency yields negligible system-level gain. Misaligned with the profiling evidence.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Implementing a 2-pass online softmax (fusing max and sum reductions) is a standard, highly effective optimization for memory-bound post-op kernels. High value and manageable risk.

strategies.intent: Enable cuDNN benchmarking and TF32 to accelerate the 3D transposed convolution.
strategies.summary: Set PyTorch backend flags to allow cuDNN to auto-tune and use Tensor Cores for the convolution.
implementation_hints: Add `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True` in the `__init__` method to trigger cuDNN auto-tuning for the convolution.
Add `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True` and `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True` to ensure Tensor Cores are utilized if available.
strategies.expected_gain: Faster execution of `nn.ConvTranspose3d` as cuDNN selects the optimal algorithm for the specific input shapes.
risk_notes: First iteration may be slower due to auto-tuning overhead.
TF32 may slightly reduce numerical precision, though typically acceptable in deep learning.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Very cheap to try and often worthwhile for fixed-shape workloads. Benchmarking and TF32 can unlock faster cuDNN engines with minimal code change, though global backend flags and first-run autotune overhead should be managed carefully.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Setting cudnn.benchmark and allow_tf32 is the cheapest intervention in the portfolio â two lines in __init__. TF32 engages tensor cores for fp32 convolutions on Ampere+ GPUs, which could reduce register pressure similarly to strategy_05 but via a backend flag rather than explicit precision control. Limited ceiling and first-iteration warmup cost, but essentially zero implementation risk.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Enabling cuDNN benchmark and TF32 is trivial to implement, but TF32 may cause the benchmark to fail strict FP32 precision checks.

strategies.summary: Cast the input and ConvTranspose3d weights to fp16 before the transposed convolution, let cuDNN select a tensor-core-accelerated HMMA kernel, then cast the output back to fp32 before the fused clamp/softmax/scale op. The NCU profile shows the cuDNN dgrad engine is register-limited at 122 registers/thread yielding occupancy of only 2 warps/SM. fp16 cuDNN paths typically use 32-48 registers/thread, which would raise occupancy to 6-8 warps and dramatically improve latency hiding against the 0.32 long-scoreboard stall ratio.
implementation_hints: In init_body, keep self.conv_transpose as float32 but also store a half-precision copy of the weight via self.conv_transpose_fp16 or use .half() at runtime

In forward_stmt_3, cast x to .half(), call self.conv_transpose with half-precision weights using F.conv_transpose3d and bias=None or explicit .half() bias, then immediately cast result back to .float()
Alternatively wrap the conv_transpose call in torch.amp.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.float16) context manager to let PyTorch manage the cast
Ensure the output is .float() before entering the fused CUDA clamp_softmax_scale_cuda call which requires float32
Verify numerical correctness: the combination of clamp then softmax means fp16 intermediate values must survive the clamp range without overflow
strategies.expected_gain: 20-40% reduction in conv_transpose runtime by replacing the 2-warp-occupancy dgrad engine with a tensor-core HMMA path at higher occupancy; overall model speedup estimated1.30-1.45x over root
risk_notes: fp16 overflow: clamp_max must not exceed ~65504; clamp_min of 0.0 is safe
cuDNN may not always select an HMMA path for all ConvTranspose3d shapes; verify with NCU that register count drops
Weight cast adds minor overhead on first forward call if done lazily; avoid repeated .half() inside the hot path
Output of fp16 conv_transpose may have slightly different numerical values; correctness tolerance check required
forbidden_patterns: Do not change avg_pool3d or the fused post-op kernel
Do not keep input x in fp16 after the conv_transpose output
Do not call .contiguous() on the fp16 tensor unless required for the fused kernel

review_notes.openai-compatible: Potentially attractive if cuDNN switches to a better tensor-core path, but numerical drift and backend variability make it less dependable. Worth testing behind a guard, not a clear default optimization.
review_notes.claude-compatible: fp16 cast around the conv-transpose to engage cuDNN HMMA tensor-core paths is well-motivated: 122 regs/thread in fp32 â expected ~32-48 in fp16, raising occupancy from 2 to 6+ warps and directly addressing the long-scoreboard stall. Implementation is compact (autocast or explicit cast), fallback is a one-line revert, and numerical risk is manageable given the downstream clamp. Best effort-to-gain ratio in the portfolio.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Casting to FP16 to force Tensor Core usage is likely to fail strict numerical correctness checks in benchmarking, despite the performance benefits.

strategies.intent: Utilize `channels_last_3d` memory format to accelerate the 3D convolution via Tensor Cores.
strategies.summary: Convert tensors to NDHWC layout for the PyTorch ops, then back to contiguous for the custom kernel.
implementation_hints: Convert the input tensor to `torch.channels_last_3d` before the `avg_pool` and `conv_transpose` operations.
Call `.contiguous()` on the output tensor right before passing it to the custom CUDA kernel to satisfy its NCDHW layout assumption.
strategies.expected_gain: Up to 2x speedup on the 3D convolution on modern GPUs due to better Tensor Core utilization with channels-last layout.
risk_notes: The overhead of calling `.contiguous()` might offset the convolution speedup if the spatial dimensions are very large.
forbidden_patterns: Passing a channels_last tensor directly to the custom kernel without modifying the kernel's indexing logic.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Too generic and likely to pay a meaningful layout-conversion cost, especially since the custom fused kernel still expects contiguous NCDHW afterward. Possible gain, but weak risk-adjusted value without proof that ConvTranspose3d improves enough to offset copies.
review_notes.claude-compatible: channels_last_3d layout conversion is a real lever but the 'up to 2x' claim is optimistic; empirical gains on ConvTranspose3d in NDHWC format are GPU- and cuDNN-version-dependent and often 5â15%. The contiguous() round-trip before the custom kernel adds overhead that may offset gains on small spatial volumes. Strategy_08 covers this ground in more detail.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Using channels_last_3d memory format is a solid framework-level optimization that can trigger faster cuDNN kernels, provided the contiguous() overhead doesn't erase the gains.

strategies.summary: Convert the tensor to NDHWC (channels_last_3d) memory format before avg_pool3d and ConvTranspose3d so cuDNN selects a spatially-local NHWDC kernel variant that reduces register pressure and improves cache line utilization. The current85% L2 throughput with only 15% DRAM throughput shows data fits in L2 but the access pattern is strided along the channel dimension; NDHWC groups spatial neighbors in cache lines, cutting bank conflicts and reducing the working set per L2 access.
implementation_hints: In forward_stmt_2, prepend x = x.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last_3d) before self.avg_pool(x); mark avg_pool with .to(memory_format=...) on output if needed
Verify self.conv_transpose(x) accepts channels_last_3d input; PyTorch's ConvTranspose3d propagates memory format automatically when the weight is also in channels_last_3d
In init_body, add self.conv_transpose = self.conv_transpose.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last_3d) after construction to prime cuDNN algorithm selection
Before calling clamp_softmax_scale_cuda, call x = x.contiguous() to ensure the fused CUDA kernel receives a contiguous NCDHW tensor as expected
Benchmark with and without the contiguous() call; if conv_transpose output is already NCDHW-contiguous, skip it
strategies.expected_gain: 5-15% gain on the conv_transpose stage by triggering a lower-register-pressure cuDNN NDHWC kernel; overall ~1.20-1.30x over root
risk_notes: The contiguous() call before clamp_softmax_scale_cuda adds a copy if the output is not already contiguous; profile to confirm it is cheaper than the register-pressure penalty
Not all GPU architectures have optimized NDHWC ConvTranspose3d paths in cuDNN; gain is architecture-dependent
avg_pool3d NDHWC support in older PyTorch/CUDA versions may fall back to a slow path; check runtime warnings
forbidden_patterns: Do not pass a non-contiguous tensor to clamp_softmax_scale_cuda
Do not change the pool kernel size, conv stride, padding, or dilation

review_notes.openai-compatible: More detailed than strategy_06, but still leans heavily on architecture-dependent NDHWC wins while adding likely `.contiguous()` overhead before the fused kernel. Better as an experiment than a high-confidence optimization path.
review_notes.claude-compatible: More rigorous treatment of channels_last_3d than strategy_06, including weight format priming and explicit contiguous() guard before the fused kernel. The L2-pattern argument is coherent. Still architecture-dependent and risks a hidden slow path in older cuDNN/PyTorch. Expected5â15% on the conv stage is real but modest; overlaps significantly with strategy_06.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Similar to strategy_06, leveraging channels_last_3d is a practical and effective way to improve cuDNN performance with minimal code changes.

strategies.summary: Replace self.conv_transpose(x) with a purpose-built CUDA kernel specialized for the exact parameters observed at runtime: in_channels=32, out_channels=64, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1, output_padding=1. A scatter-accumulate kernel over the output tensor, where each output thread owns one output voxel and gathers contributing input voxels, can be written with explicit register budgeting targetingâ¤48 registers/thread to raise occupancy from the current 2 warps to 6+ warps per SM, directly addressing the dominant stall.
implementation_hints: Use a grid of (N, C_out, ceil(D_out*H_out*W_out/BLOCK)) blocks; each thread computes one output element by iterating over the3x3x3 kernel window in the input
Pre-compute the valid input coordinate check for boundary handling using closed-form expressions: in_d = (out_d + padding - kd) where stride divides evenly â this avoids divergent branches
Store weight in __constant__ memory if weight size fits (32*64*3*3*3*4 = 576KB â too large for constant memory); instead use shared memory prefetch of the weight slice for the current C_out block
Use __launch_bounds__(BLOCK, MIN_BLOCKS) with BLOCK=128 and MIN_BLOCKS=4 to hint the compiler to constrain register allocation
Load weight for the current output channel block into shared memory cooperatively before the inner loop to reduce global memory pressure on the L2
Export the kernel as convtranspose3d_k3s2_cuda and call it from forward_stmt_3 after checking is_cuda, dtype, and contiguity
strategies.expected_gain: 25-50% reduction in conv_transpose runtime if occupancy rises from 2 to 5+ warps; overall ~1.35-1.55x over root assuming correct boundary handling
risk_notes: Correctness is sensitive to padding, output_padding, and stride; test against F.conv_transpose3d reference with tolerance 1e-4
The weight tensor from nn.ConvTranspose3d has shape (in_channels, out_channels/groups, kD, kH, kW) â note the dimension order is different from forward conv
Shared memory usage for weight tiles must not exceed device limit; for out_channels=64 and kernel=3^3=27, weight slice per block is 64*27*4=6912 bytes per block â safe
This is high-complexity; incorrect boundary indexing will produce silent numerical errors rather than crashes
forbidden_patterns: Do not change avg_pool3d or the fused post-op kernel
Do not generalize to arbitrary kernel sizes at the cost of register count
Do not use atomicAdd on the output unless throughput analysis justifies it over the output-stationary gather pattern

review_notes.openai-compatible: Directly attacks the main bottleneck and the register-pressure diagnosis is plausible, but this is a high-effort, high-correctness-risk custom kernel. Could be excellent if tuned well, yet risk-adjusted value is only moderate versus safer dispatch/autotune options.
review_notes.claude-compatible: The most detailed custom conv-transpose proposal in the portfolio: explicit output-stationary gather pattern, __launch_bounds__ for register capping, shared memory weight tile sizing worked out, and correct note about nn.ConvTranspose3d weight dimension order (in_channels, out_channels/groups, kD, kH, kW). Directly targets the 2-warp occupancy ceiling. Scored 4 rather than 5 because correctness risk is high â padding/output_padding indexing errors are silent â and shared memory at 576KB for weights exceeds constant memory, requiring careful block-level tiling.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: A custom scatter-accumulate kernel for conv_transpose3d is extremely error-prone (especially with boundary conditions) and unlikely to outperform highly tuned vendor libraries.

strategies.intent: Replace the cuDNN transposed-convolution with a lower-register implicit-GEMM style kernel tuned for the fixed benchmark shape to improve occupancy.
strategies.summary: NCU evidence shows the active conv-transpose engine is constrained by register usage (`launch__registers_per_thread=122`, `launch__occupancy_limit_registers=2`) and exhibits long latency stalls, while memory bandwidth is far from saturated. That is a classic sign that a shape-specialized kernel with simpler inner loops, smaller per-thread state, and more resident warps could beat the generic backend kernel even without increasing DRAM traffic. Given the fixed execution facts, a narrow implicit-GEMM or direct-deconvolution kernel specialized to the benchmark parameters is a viable reroot candidate.
implementation_hints: Specialize for the known `kernel_size=3`, `stride=2`, `padding=1`, `output_padding=1` tuple to shrink index math and reduce live registers.
Favor a tile mapping that gives each thread fewer accumulators so occupancy rises relative to the cuDNN engine.
Use constant-memory or read-only-cache access for weights when the filter footprint is small enough.
Keep the champion fused clamp/softmax/scale kernel as the downstream consumer so only the producer changes.
Provide a strict fallback to `self.conv_transpose(x)` outside the specialized regime.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate to high if the specialized kernel materially lowers register pressure and raises resident warps; especially attractive because the current main kernel is underutilizing SMs.
risk_notes: Much narrower applicability than an algorithm-dispatch approach.
Performance can regress if the tiling underuses tensor cores or causes excess atomic/update traffic.
Verification burden is higher because transposed-convolution indexing is easy to get subtly wrong.
memory_methods: Exploit small fixed filter size for cached weight reads.
forbidden_patterns: Do not use atomics-heavy scatter formulations unless they are shape-proven faster.
Do not increase register pressure beyond the current backend path.
Do not alter NCHW/NCDHW semantics at the Python boundary.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Well aligned with the register-limited cuDNN profile and could pay off, but writing a specialized transposed-convolution kernel is expensive and correctness-sensitive. Strong upside, weaker risk-adjusted value than dispatch-based approaches.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Implicit-GEMM specialized for the fixed parameter tuple targets the same root cause as strategy_01 and strategy_09 but is less detailed and carries all the same correctness risk with less concrete implementation guidance. Moderate score reflects valid direction but higher uncertainty without explicit tiling or register budget.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Writing a custom implicit-GEMM conv_transpose3d kernel from scratch is highly complex and very likely to underperform cuDNN or fail correctness checks.

strategies.intent: Increase instruction-level parallelism (ILP) in the custom CUDA kernel by explicitly unrolling the grid-stride loops.
strategies.summary: Process multiple `float4` elements per thread in the inner loops to hide instruction latency.
implementation_hints: In the vectorized kernel, load and process 2 or 4 `float4` elements per thread in each loop iteration.
Accumulate max and sum in independent registers (e.g., `local_max1`, `local_max2`) before combining them at the end of the loop.
Use `#pragma unroll` for the inner processing steps.
strategies.expected_gain: Better hiding of arithmetic and memory latencies, improving SM throughput.
risk_notes: Increased register pressure could lower occupancy, though the current kernel has plenty of headroom (occupancy limit registers: 2).

review_notes.openai-compatible: Reasonable micro-optimization for the custom post-op kernel, but it does not address the dominant transposed-convolution cost. Extra unrolling may also increase register pressure for a relatively small end-to-end payoff.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Loop unrolling and float4 ILP for the custom post-op kernel addresses a kernel that is not the system bottleneck. The note that 'the current kernel has plenty of headroom (occupancy limit registers: 2)' is actually evidence that ILP is not the binding constraint for that kernel. Correct technique applied to the wrong target.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Increasing ILP via float4 vectorization and loop unrolling in the custom post-op kernel is a proven technique to maximize memory bandwidth utilization.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l2_p38_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():
    global _STARK_EXTENSION
    if _STARK_EXTENSION is None:
        _STARK_EXTENSION = load_inline(
            name=_stark_extension_name(),
            cpp_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC),
            cuda_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC),
            functions=None,
            extra_cflags=['-O3'],
            extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3', '--use_fast_math'],
            with_cuda=True,
            verbose=False,
        )
    return _STARK_EXTENSION

# <<<IMPROVE:user_helpers>>>
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

CUDA_CPP_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cpp>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>

// Add pybind exports for custom CUDA entrypoints here.
PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) {}
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

CUDA_CU_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cu>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>
#include <cuda.h>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Add CUDA kernels and exported wrapper functions here.
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

class ModelNew(nn.Module):
    """
        Model that performs average pooling, 3D transposed convolution, clamping,
        spatial softmax, and multiplication by a learnable scale.
        """
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride, padding, output_padding, pool_kernel_size, clamp_min, clamp_max):
        super().__init__()
        # <<<IMPROVE:init_body>>>
        self.avg_pool = nn.AvgPool3d(pool_kernel_size)
        self.conv_transpose = nn.ConvTranspose3d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride=stride, padding=padding, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.clamp_min = clamp_min
        self.clamp_max = clamp_max
        self.scale = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(1, out_channels, 1, 1, 1))
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

    def forward(self, x):
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_1>>>
        # Baseline fallback keeps the official PyTorch forward path.
        # After implementing CUDA_CPP_SRC / CUDA_CU_SRC, call _stark_get_extension().your_entrypoint(...).
        """
                Args:
                    x (torch.Tensor): Input tensor of shape (batch_size, in_channels, depth, height, width).

                Returns:
                    torch.Tensor: Output tensor of shape (batch_size, out_channels, depth, height, width).
                """
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_2>>>
        x = self.avg_pool(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_3>>>
        x = self.conv_transpose(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_4>>>
        x = torch.clamp(x, self.clamp_min, self.clamp_max)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_5>>>
        b, c, d, h, w = x.shape
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_6>>>
        x = x.view(b, c, -1)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_7>>>
        x = torch.softmax(x, dim=2)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_8>>>
        x = x.view(b, c, d, h, w)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_9>>>
        x = x * self.scale
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_10>>>
        return x
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
